paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="6C20444E" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="007850D9" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00A21757"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">{{FIG:3}} shows an example of a transformer model, namely transformer {{fig}}00, according to aspects of the present disclosure. Transformer {{fig}}00 depicts a decoder-only architecture designed to process sequences of data, such as natural language text or image patches, by transforming input representations into contextualized output representations. Embodiments of transformer {{fig}}00 include a diffusion transformer as described with reference to FIG. {{FIG:6}}, and transformer {{fig}}00 can be used as a backbone e.g. for </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:eastAsia="SimSun"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">guided latent diffusion model </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">{{figref:4}}00</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:eastAsia="SimSun"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some embodiments, transformer {{fig}}00 includes aspects or examples of, or are modified as described for, media processing system or media generation model according to the present disclosure (referring to FIGs. {{FIG:1}}-2).</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="2CE96750" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="00366D26" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some embodiments, transformer {{fig}}00 includes input token vectors, operation {{fig}}25, position embedding {{fig}}30, decoder blocks {{fig}}35, output token vectors, and token classification head {{fig}}82. In the example shown, input token vectors include first input token {{fig}}05, second input token {{fig}}10, third input token {{fig}}15, and fourth input token {{fig}}20; correspondingly, output token vectors include first output token {{fig}}65, second output token {{fig}}70, third output token {{fig}}75, and fourth output token {{fig}}80. Decoder blocks {{fig}}35 includes a set of blocks (typically at least 3, e.g. 12, 24, or 48) stacked together, each of the set of blocks having an architecture identical or similar to a decoder block {{fig}}40. As depicted, Decoder block {{fig}}40 includes layer norm {{fig}}45, attention {{fig}}50, FFNN {{fig}}55 (feed-forward neural network), and operation {{fig}}60. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="112D2F06" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">At an input representation layer, transformer {{fig}}00 generates the input token vectors (first input token {{fig}}05 through fourth input token {{fig}}20) that represent initial embeddings of discrete input tokens (e.g., words, subwords, or image patches) into a continuous vector space, such as </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSup><m:sSupPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSupPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:scr m:val="double-struck"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>R</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> for an embedding dimension </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. For an input sequence of length </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>L</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> (e.g. </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>L = 4</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> as depicted), the input token vectors can be viewed as a matrix </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">X </m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">∈ </m:t></m:r><m:sSup><m:sSupPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSupPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:scr m:val="double-struck"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>R</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>L</m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>×</m:t></m:r><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>.</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="5D0D99CC" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="00860504" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Position embedding {{fig}}30 is fed to decoder blocks {{fig}}35, each having an architecture identical or similar to that of the decoder block {{fig}}40. Decoder block {{fig}}40 includes several sub-layers. Layer norm {{fig}}45 normalizes the activations or states across the feature dimension for each token independently. This stabilizes the learning process, prevents gradients from exploding or vanishing, and allows for smoother optimization across deep networks. In some embodiments, for each input vector </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">x </m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">∈ </m:t></m:r><m:sSup><m:sSupPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSupPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:scr m:val="double-struck"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>R</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">(e.g. first input token {{fig}}05, second input token {{fig}}10, third input token {{fig}}15, or fourth input token {{fig}}15 at the bottom instance of layer norm {{fig}}45, or a corresponding hidden state at the top instance), layer norm {{fig}}45 computes:</w:t></w:r></w:p>

items.name: a guided latent diffusion model
paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="62E2DFE0" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. {{FIG:4}} shows an example of a guided latent diffusion model according to aspects of the present disclosure. Diffusion models are a class of generative neural networks which can be trained to generate new data with features similar to features found in training data. In particular, diffusion models can be used to generate novel images. Diffusion models can be used for various image generation tasks including image super-resolution, generation of images with perceptual metrics, conditional generation (e.g., generation based on text guidance), image inpainting, and image manipulation. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="34B38598" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Types of diffusion models include Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) and Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIMs). In DDPMs, the generative process includes reversing a stochastic Markov diffusion process. DDIMs, on the other hand, use a deterministic process so that the same input results in the same output. Diffusion models may also be characterized by whether the noise is added to the image itself, or to image features generated by an encoder (i.e., latent diffusion).</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="6618DD4D" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Diffusion models work by iteratively adding noise to the data during a forward process and then learning to recover the data by denoising the data during a reverse process. </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">For example, during training, guided latent diffusion model {{fig}}00 may take an original image {{fig}}05 in a pixel space {{fig}}10 as input and apply and image encoder {{fig}}15 to convert original image {{fig}}05 into original image features {{fig}}20 in a latent space {{fig}}25. Then, a forward diffusion process {{fig}}30 gradually adds noise to the original image features {{fig}}20 to obtain noisy features {{fig}}35 (also in latent space {{fig}}25) at various noise levels. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="62EEBEF1" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Next, a reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40 (e.g., a U-Net ANN) gradually removes the noise from the noisy features {{fig}}35 at the various noise levels to obtain denoised image features {{fig}}45 in latent space {{fig}}25. In some examples, the denoised image features {{fig}}45 are compared to the original image features {{fig}}20 at each of the various noise levels, and parameters of the reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40 of the diffusion model are updated based on the comparison. Finally, an image decoder {{fig}}50 decodes the denoised image features {{fig}}45 to obtain an output image {{fig}}55 in pixel space {{fig}}10. In some cases, an output image {{fig}}55 is created at each of the various noise levels. The output image {{fig}}55 can be compared to the original image {{fig}}05 to train the reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="7C2019EF" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, image encoder {{fig}}15 and image decoder {{fig}}50 are pre-trained prior to training the reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40. In some examples, they are trained jointly, or the image encoder {{fig}}15 and image decoder {{fig}}50 and fine-tuned jointly with the reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="768FE5B9" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40 can also be guided based on a text prompt {{fig}}60, or another guidance prompt, such as an image, a layout, a segmentation map, etc. The text prompt {{fig}}60 can be encoded using a text encoder {{fig}}65 (e.g., a multimodal encoder) to obtain guidance features {{fig}}70 in guidance space {{fig}}75. The guidance features {{fig}}70 can be combined with the noisy features {{fig}}35 at one or more layers of the reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40 to ensure that the output image {{fig}}55 includes content described by the text prompt {{fig}}60. For example, guidance </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>features {{fig}}70 can be combined with the noisy features {{fig}}35 using a cross-attention block within the reverse diffusion process {{fig}}40.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

items.name: a U-Net
paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="096CECD0" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. {{FIG:5}} shows an example of a U-Net {{fig}}00 according to aspects of the present disclosure. In some examples, U-Net {{fig}}00 is an example of the component that performs the reverse diffusion process {{figref:4}}40 of guided diffusion model {{figref:4}}00 described with reference to FIG. {{FIG:4}}. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="32C58BC1" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some examples, diffusion models are based on a neural network architecture known as a U-Net. The U-Net {{fig}}00 takes input features {{fig}}05 having an initial resolution and an initial number of channels and processes the input features {{fig}}05 using an initial neural network layer {{fig}}10 (e.g., a convolutional network layer) to produce intermediate features {{fig}}15. The intermediate features {{fig}}15 are then down-sampled using a down-sampling layer {{fig}}20 such that down-sampled features {{fig}}25 have a resolution less than the initial resolution and a number of channels greater than the initial number of channels. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="5F8F3AAF" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">This process is repeated multiple times, and then the process is reversed. That is, the down-sampled features {{fig}}25 are up-sampled using up-sampling process {{fig}}30 to obtain up-sampled features {{fig}}35. The up-sampled features {{fig}}35 can be combined with intermediate features {{fig}}15 having a same resolution and number of channels via a skip connection {{fig}}40. These inputs are processed using a final neural network layer {{fig}}45 to produce output features {{fig}}50. In some cases, the output features {{fig}}50 have the same resolution as the initial resolution and the same number of channels as the initial number of channels.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="14CB4808" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, U-Net {{fig}}00 takes additional input features to produce conditionally generated output. For example, the additional input features could include a vector representation of an input prompt. The additional input features can be combined with the intermediate features {{fig}}15 within the neural network at one or more layers. For example, a cross-</w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">attention module can be used to combine the additional input features and the intermediate features {{fig}}15. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

items.name: a diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture
paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="5597296E" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. {{FIG:6}} shows an example of a diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture according to aspects of the present disclosure. While some generative diffusion models are based on a convolutional layer backbone (e.g., the U-Net), others may be based on a transformer network backbone. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="231D4897" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The example shown includes predicted noise {{fig}}05, predicted covariance {{fig}}10, linear and reshape layers {{fig}}15, normalization layer {{fig}}20, DiT block(s) {{fig}}25, patchify operation {{fig}}30, embedding {{fig}}35, noised latent {{fig}}40, timestep information {{fig}}45, label information {{fig}}50, and an implementation of one block in the DiT block(s) {{fig}}25 by a DiT Block {{fig}}96. The DiT Block {{fig}}96 includes: second residual connection {{fig}}60, second scaling operations {{fig}}62, feed-forward network {{fig}}64, post-normalization second scaling and shifting {{fig}}66, second normalization {{fig}}68, first residual connection {{fig}}70, first scaling operations {{fig}}72, self-attention {{fig}}74, post-normalization first scaling and shifting {{fig}}76, first normalization {{fig}}78, input tokens {{fig}}80, conditioning tokens {{fig}}82, multi-layer perceptron (MLP) {{fig}}84, post-normalization first scaling and shifting parameters {{fig}}86, first scaling parameter {{fig}}88, post-normalization second scaling and shifting parameters {{fig}}90, and second scaling parameter {{fig}}92. In some embodiments, the architecture uses a Latent Diffusion Transformer {{fig}}94. In some embodiments, DiT Block {{fig}}96 uses an “adaLN-Zero” technique.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="35768459" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) is a popular architecture for diffusion models and is designed to be structurally faithful to standard transformer architecture. DiT incorporates transformer structures’ scaling properties. For training denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) of images (e.g., spatial representations of images), DiT is based on a Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture which operates on sequences of patches. DiT processes images </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">by dividing them into patches, converting these patches into tokens, and applying attention mechanisms to model relationships between different regions of the image. This approach allows the model to capture both local and long-range dependencies in the image generation process. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="1EC02CB7" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, input to DiT is a spatial representation </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>z</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. For </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>256×256×3</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> images, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>z</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> has shape </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>32×32×4</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. A first layer of a DiT is to carry out patchify operation, where the DiT divides an input image into patches and converts the patches (a form of spatial input) into a sequence of </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>T</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> tokens, each of dimension </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, by linearly embedding each patch in the input. Following the patchify process, ViT frequency-based positional embeddings are applied to all input tokens. In some cases, the number of tokens </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>T</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> created by patchify is determined by a patch size hyperparameter </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. In some cases, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>T=</m:t></m:r><m:sSup><m:sSupPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSupPr><m:e><m:d><m:dPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:dPr><m:e><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>I</m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:lit/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>/</m:t></m:r><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:e></m:d></m:e><m:sup><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, where </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>I</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is another shape parameter, thus halving </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> will quadruple </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>T</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, which in some cases at least quadruples total of transformer Giga Floating Point Operations (Gflops). Accordingly, embodiments herein can increase inference speed by configuring and operating within a highly compressed latent space, resulting in fewer processed tokens relative to higher spatial dimension (e.g., H x W) spaces. In some examples, changing </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> has no impact on downstream parameter counts, i.e., parameter counts in downstream layers of DiT is independent from </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. In some examples, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">p=2, 4 </m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">or </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>8.</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> Various patch sizes, transformer block architectures and model sizes are implemented.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="4D802EEA" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Following Patchify operation, attention mechanisms are applied to model relationships between different regions of the image in one or more DiT blocks. In addition to noised image inputs, diffusion models sometimes process additional conditional information such as noise timesteps </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>t</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, class labels </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>c</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, natural language information, etc. Four variants of transformer blocks for processing conditional inputs including both input information and conditional information are described below. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="499496F5" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, DiT blocks in the DiT network are implemented using adaptive layer norm (adaLN) blocks. Following adaptive normalization layers in generative adversarial networks (GANs) and conventional diffusion models with U-Net backbones, in some examples, standard normalization layers in transformer blocks are replaced with adaptive layer norm (adaLN). Rather than directly learning dimension-wise scale </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and shift parameters </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, in adaLN the system regresses </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> from a sum of the embedding vectors of the noise timesteps </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>t</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and the class labels </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>c</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. An adaLN adds relatively small numbers of Gflops and is more efficient. Additionally, adaLN is a conditioning mechanism that applies a same function to all tokens.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="64700793" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, DiT blocks in the DiT network are implemented using adaLN-Zero blocks, which leverages zero-initialization techniques. In Residual Networks (ResNets), initializing each residual block as the identity function </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">x </m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>↦</m:t></m:r><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>x</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is beneficial. In some examples, zero-initializing a final batch norm scale factor </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> in each block accelerates large-scale training in supervised learning settings. Diffusion models based on U-Nets use a similar initialization strategy, zero-initializing final convolutional layer in each block prior to residual connections. An adaLN-Zero block is modified from an adaLN block using similar zero-initialization techniques. In addition to regressing the dimension-wise scale </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and the shifting parameters </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, the system also regresses dimension-wise scaling parameters </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>αs</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> that are applied immediately prior to residual connections within the DiT block. The network initializes a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to output a zero-vector for all </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>α</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">s; this initializes an entire DiT block as the identity function. As with the adaLN block, adaLNZero adds negligible Gflops to the model.</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/><w:iCs/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve"> </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="38DF72B0" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, DiT blocks in the DiT network are implemented using in-context conditioning, where vector embeddings of </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>t</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>c</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> are appended as two additional tokens in the input sequence, and after a final block, the network removes the two conditioning tokens from the sequence.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="6F3F8D12" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, DiT blocks in the DiT network include cross-attention blocks. The DiT network concatenates the embeddings of </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>t</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>c</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> into a length-two sequence, separate from the image token sequence. The transformer block is modified to include an additional multi-head cross-attention layer following the multi-head self-attention block. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="7413E226" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some cases, the DiT network includes a sequence of </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>N</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> DiT blocks, each operating at a hidden dimension size </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. Following ViT, the DiT network uses standard transformer configs that jointly scale </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>N</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and attention heads. In some examples, Small (S), Base (B), Large (L) variants, XLarge (XL) variants of model sizes are implemented. Small or Base model sizes have </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>N=12</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> layers of DiT blocks, Large model sizes have 24 layers of DiT blocks. XLarge model sizes have 28 layers of DiT blocks.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="39D7BA53" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">After a final DiT block, the DiT network decodes the sequence of image tokens into an output noise prediction and an output diagonal covariance prediction. Both outputs have shapes equal to an original spatial input. Standard linear decoder is utilized to decode, wherein a final normalization layer (or adaptive normalization layer if the DiT block is an adaLN block) and linearly decode each token into a </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>×</m:t></m:r><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve">p </m:t></m:r><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>×</m:t></m:r><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2C</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> tensor, where </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>C</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is a number of channels in the spatial input to the DiT network and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is the patch size hyperparameter. Finally, decoded tokens are rearranged into their original spatial layout to get the predicted noise and covariance.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="2413D8FF" w14:textId="0E108D6A" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The architecture {{fig}}00, in some cases, uses a Latent Diffusion Transformer {{fig}}94. The architecture {{fig}}00 processes noised latent {{fig}}40, which may be a noised version of an input image encoded in a latent space. Patchify operation {{fig}}30 divides the noised latent into a sequence of patches that are processed as tokens. The tokens are vector representations of each patch of the image in latent space and are adjusted through attention processes. Each of the tokens also receives timestep information {{fig}}45 and label information {{fig}}50 and, accordingly, their embedding {{fig}}35, which encodes the current denoising timestep and class labels as conditional information. </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>In some cases, embedding {{fig}}35 is referred to as conditional embedding or conditional information embedding. In some cases, a positional embedding which encodes each token</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">’s spatial position in the image is applied to the patchified input tokens at the patchify operations {{fig}}30. In some examples the positional embedding is ViT frequency-based positional embedding. The input tokens {{fig}}80 generated by the patchify operation {{fig}}30 and the conditioning tokens {{fig}}82 generated by the embedding {{fig}}35 are processed through N DiT block(s) {{fig}}25, where N may be 12, 24 or 28. Other values of N may be used. In some cases, conditional tokens refer to tokens generated based on embedding {{fig}}35 encoding timestep information {{fig}}45 and label information {{fig}}50. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="2878761F" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Each of the DiT block(s) {{fig}}25 includes multiple processing stages. DiT Block {{fig}}96 illustrates an embodiment of one block in the DiT block(s) {{fig}}25. In some embodiments, the DiT Block {{fig}}96 is an example of, or includes aspects of, the adaLN-Zero block. In some cases, input tokens {{fig}}80 interact with the conditioning tokens {{fig}}82 through multiple attention mechanisms. Particularly, after first normalization {{fig}}78 applied to the input tokens and MLP {{fig}}84 to the conditional tokens, MLP {{fig}}84 generates or updates post-normalization first scaling and shifting parameters {{fig}}86, denoted as </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>,</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, for post-normalization first scaling and shifting {{fig}}76 to scale and shift the output of first normalization {{fig}}78 accordingly. As the normalized input tokens obtained from first normalization {{fig}}78 are scaled and shifted at post-normalization first scaling and shifting {{fig}}76 using the conditional information carried as least in </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>,</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, this allows the input information and conditional information to interact. Self-attention {{fig}}74 allows the scaled and shifted normalized input tokens, namely the output from post-normalization first scaling and shifting {{fig}}76, to attend to each other. MLP {{fig}}84 also generates or updates first scaling parameter {{fig}}88 denoted as </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>α</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> for first scaling operations {{fig}}72 to scale the output of self-attention {{fig}}74 (e.g., multi-head self-attention), further interacting the input information and conditional information. The input tokens {{fig}}80 is then summed with the output of first scaling operations </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="002C7A47"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">{{fig}}72 at first residual connection {{fig}}70. In some examples, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>α</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> has initial values 0, and the DiT Block {{fig}}96 is initialized as the identity function.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="305841AE" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">A similar process is performed in a second half of the DiT Block {{fig}}96. MLP {{fig}}84 generates or updates post-normalization second scaling and shifting parameters {{fig}}90, denoted as </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>,</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, for post-normalization second scaling and shifting {{fig}}66 to scale and shift the output of second normalization {{fig}}68 accordingly. As the output from second normalization {{fig}}68 is scaled and shifted using the conditional information carried at least in </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>γ</m:t></m:r><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>,</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/><w:i/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>β</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, this allows the input information and conditional information to further interact. Feed-forward network {{fig}}64 then processes the scaled and shifted output from post-normalization second scaling and shifting {{fig}}66. MLP {{fig}}84 also generates or updates second scaling parameter {{fig}}92 denoted as </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>α</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> for second scaling operations {{fig}}62 to scale the output of feed-forward network {{fig}}64, further interacting the input information and conditional information. In some cases, the feed-forward network {{fig}}64 is a pointwise feed-forward network. The output from first residual connection {{fig}}70 is then summed with the output of second scaling operations {{fig}}62 at second residual connection {{fig}}60, and the result is the final output of DiT Block {{fig}}96. In some examples, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>α</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> has initial values 0, and the DiT Block {{fig}}96 is initialized as the identity function. This process repeats for each DiT block in the sequence.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="44DC6F73" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">After processing through all DiT block(s) {{fig}}25, the outputs undergo normalization layer {{fig}}20 followed by linear and reshape layers {{fig}}15. The final output is the predicted noise {{fig}}05, which represents the model’s prediction of the noise that was added to initially create the noised latent {{fig}}40, and the predicted covariance {{fig}}10, which represents the model’s prediction of the covariance. The predicted noise {{fig}}05 is removed from noised latent {{fig}}40 at each diffusion timestep, and the predicted covariance may affect how noise is removed or resampled in the reverse or denoising process. At the end of the denoising schedule, the latent sample is decoded to generate the synthetic image in pixel space.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

In some examples, denoising process {{fig}}00 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:color w:val="000000"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">describes the reverse diffusion process {{figref:4}}40 of </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">guided diffusion model {{figref:4}}00 described with reference to FIG. {{FIG:4}}. Although the following description uses the term “diffusion process” for consistency with FIG. {{FIG:7}}, the techniques described herein encompass both diffusion-based and flow-matching-based training and inference formulations, as described in greater detail below.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="0DF6B2E6" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRPr="002C7A47" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">As described above with reference to FIG. {{FIG:4}}, using a diffusion model can involve both a forward diffusion process {{fig}}05 for adding noise to an image (or features in a latent space) and a reverse diffusion process {{fig}}10 for denoising the images (or features) to obtain a denoised image. <w:p w14:paraId="6088455B" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00637AAA" w:rsidRDefault="00637AAA" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">At inference time under the flow matching formulation, generation proceeds by drawing a sample from the noise distribution at t = 1 and integrating the learned velocity field backward from t = 1 to t = 0 using a numerical ODE solver such as an Euler method or a higher-order solver. This is analogous to reverse diffusion process {{fig}}10 in that the neural network iteratively transforms noise into coherent latent structure, but the integration follows a deterministic ODE trajectory rather than a stochastic reverse Markov chain. In practice, the </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="00546DCC"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">straight-line interpolation paths of Equation </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">10 may require fewer integration steps to achieve comparable generation quality relative to the curved trajectories implied by typical diffusion noise schedules, which can reduce inference cost for high-resolution image and video generation.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="0338A12E" w14:textId="59B13CFB" w:rsidR="00D23356" w:rsidRDefault="00D23356" w:rsidP="00637AAA"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some embodiments of the present disclosure, the media generation model is configured to generate a matte video in a single forward pass rather than through an iterative reverse process such as reverse diffusion process {{fig}}10 of FIG. {{FIG:7}} or the multi-step ODE integration of the flow matching formulation. In place of a sequence of denoising steps, the denoising network of the media generation model maps a noised latent and a conditioning input directly to a clean latent at a single timestep. The conditioning input includes a latent representation of an input video and a latent representation of a binary mask, and the single forward pass produces a latent representation of a matte video. In some embodiments, the denoising network is parameterized to predict a clean latent or to predict a velocity, e.g., under a v-parameterization, such that the prediction at the single timestep corresponds to the clean matte latent rather than to an intermediate noise estimate. Generating a matte video in a single </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidR="00434988" w:rsidRPr="00434988"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>forward pass reduces the number of forward evaluations of the denoising network relative to a multi-step formulation, which increases inference speed for high-resolution video</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="48E9D39D" w14:textId="1D989D8B" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00414334"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">{{FIG:14}} is a flow diagram depicting an algorithm as a step-by-step procedure {{fig}}00 in an example implementation of operations performable for training a machine-learning model.  In some embodiments, the procedure {{fig}}00 describes an operation of configuring the media generation model as described with reference to FIG. {{FIG:2}}. The procedure {{fig}}00 provides one or more examples of generating training data, use of the training data to train a machine-learning model, and use of the trained machine-learning model to perform a task.  </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="4D680A32" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">To begin in this example, a machine-learning system collects training data (block {{fig}}02) that is to be used as a basis to train a machine-learning model, i.e., which defines what is being modeled.  The training data is collectable by the machine-learning system from a variety of sources.  Examples of training data sources include public datasets, service provider system platforms that expose application programming interfaces (e.g., social media platforms), user data collection systems (e.g., digital surveys and online crowdsourcing systems), and so forth.  Training data collection may also include data augmentation and synthetic data generation techniques to expand and diversify available training data, balancing techniques to balance a number of positive and negative examples, and so forth.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="2B5C0A0A" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The machine-learning system is also configurable to identify features that are relevant (block {{fig}}04) to a type of task, for which the machine-learning model is to be trained.  Task examples include classification, natural language processing, generative artificial intelligence, recommendation engines, reinforcement learning, clustering, and so forth.  To do so, the machine-learning system collects the training data based on the identified features and/or filters the training data based on the identified features after collection.  The training data is then utilized to train a machine-learning model.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="04F9EE5D" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In order to train the machine-learning model in the illustrated example, the machine-learning model is first initialized (block {{fig}}06).  Initialization of the machine-learning model </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="00414334"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">includes selecting a model architecture (block </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">{{fig}}08) to be trained.  Examples of model architectures include neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks, transformer networks, generative adversarial networks (GANs), decision trees, support vector machines, linear regression, logistic regression, Bayesian networks, random forest learning, dimensionality reduction algorithms, boosting algorithms, deep learning neural networks, etc.  </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="033A1944" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">A loss function is also selected (block {{fig}}10).  The loss function is utilized to measure a difference between an output of the machine-learning model (i.e., predictions) and target values (e.g., as expressed by the training data) to be used to train the machine-learning model.  Additionally, an optimization algorithm is selected ({{fig}}12) that is to be used in conjunction with the loss function to optimize parameters of the machine-learning model during training, examples of which include gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and so forth.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="66E7F102" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Initialization of the machine-learning model further includes setting initial values of the machine-learning model (block {{fig}}16) examples of which includes initializing weights and biases of nodes to improve efficiency in training and computational resources consumption as part of training.  Hyperparameters are also set (block {{fig}}14) that are used to control training of the machine learning model, examples of which include regularization parameters, model parameters (e.g., a number of layers in a neural network), learning rate, batch sizes selected from the training data, and so on.  The hyperparameters are set using a variety of techniques, including use of a randomization technique, through use of heuristics learned from other training scenarios, and so forth. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="6B15D97B" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The machine-learning model is then trained using the training data (block {{fig}}18) by the machine-learning system.  A machine-learning model refers to a computer representation </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="00414334"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">that can be tuned (e.g., trained and retrained) based on inputs of the training data to approximate unknown functions.  In particular, the term machine-learning model can include a model that utilizes algorithms (e.g., using the model architectures described above) to learn from, and make predictions on, known data by analyzing training data to learn and relearn to generate outputs that reflect patterns and attributes expressed by the training data.  </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="404528E9" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Examples of training types include supervised learning that employs labeled data, unsupervised learning that involves finding underlying structures or patterns within the training data, reinforcement learning based on optimization functions (e.g., rewards and/or penalties), use of nodes as part of “deep learning,” and so forth.  The machine-learning model, for instance, is configurable as including a plurality of nodes that collectively form a plurality of layers.  The layers, for instance, are configurable to include an input layer, an output layer, and one or more hidden layers.  Calculations are performed by the nodes within the layers through the hidden states through a system of weighted connections that are “learned” during training, e.g., through use of the selected loss function and backpropagation to optimize performance of the machine-learning model to perform an associated task.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="383F5BC5" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">As part of training the machine-learning model, a determination is made as to whether a stopping criterion is met (decision block {{fig}}20), i.e., which is used to validate the machine-learning model.  The stopping criterion is usable to reduce overfitting of the machine-learning model, reduce computational resource consumption, and promote an ability of the machine-learning model to address previously unseen data, i.e., that is not included specifically as an example in the training data.  Examples of a stopping criterion include but are not limited to a predefined number of epochs, validation loss stabilization, achievement of a performance improvement threshold, whether a threshold level of accuracy has been met, or based on performance metrics such as precision and recall.  If the stopping criterion has not been met </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="00414334"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>(</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">“no” from decision block {{fig}}20), the procedure {{fig}}00 continues training of the machine-learning model using the training data (block {{fig}}18) in this example.  </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="71B06855" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">If the stopping criterion is met (“yes” from decision block {{fig}}20), the trained machine-learning model is then utilized to generate an output based on subsequent data (block {{fig}}22).  The trained machine-learning model, for instance, is trained to perform a task as described above and therefore, once trained is configured to perform that task based on subsequent data received as an input and processed by the machine-learning model. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

items.name: a method for training a denoising network
paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="179F87EE" w14:textId="317A10E6" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. {{FIG:15}} shows an example of a method {{fig}}00 for training a denoising network according to aspects of the present disclosure. In some embodiments, the method {{fig}}00 describes an operation for configuring the media generation model as described with reference to FIG. {{FIG:2}}. The method {{fig}}00 represents an example for training a reverse diffusion process as described above with reference to FIGs. {{FIG:4}} and {{FIG:7}}. In some examples, these operations are performed by a system including a processor executing a set of codes to control functional elements of an apparatus, such as the guided diffusion model described in FIG. {{FIG:4}}. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="5E2E8376" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Additionally or alternatively, certain processes of method {{fig}}00 may be performed using special-purpose hardware. Generally, these operations are performed according to the methods and processes described in accordance with aspects of the present disclosure. In some cases, the operations described herein are composed of various substeps or are performed in conjunction with other operations.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="39762314" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">At operation {{fig}}05, the user initializes an untrained model. Initialization can include defining the architecture of the model and establishing initial values for the model parameters. In some cases, the initialization can include defining hyper-parameters such as the number of layers, the resolution and channels of each layer blocks, the location of skip connections, and the like.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="042C8E9C" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidRPr="00414334"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t xml:space="preserve">At operation </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">{{fig}}10, the system adds noise to a training image using a forward diffusion process in</w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve"> N</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> stages. In some cases, the forward diffusion process is a fixed process where Gaussian noise is successively added to an image. In latent diffusion models, the Gaussian noise may be successively added to features in a latent space.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="3C67B011" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">At operation {{fig}}15, the system at each stage </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>n</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, starting with stage </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>N</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, a reverse diffusion process is used to predict the image or image features at stage </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>n - 1</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">.  For example, the reverse diffusion process can predict the noise that was added by the forward diffusion process, and the predicted noise can be removed from the image to obtain the predicted image. In some cases, an original image is predicted at each stage of the training process.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="70DA5B42" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">At operation {{fig}}20, the system compares predicted image (or image features) at stage </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>n - 1</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> to an actual image (or image features), such as the image at stage</w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t xml:space="preserve"> n - 1</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> or the original input image. For example, given observed data </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>x</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, the diffusion model may be trained to minimize the variational upper bound of the negative log-likelihood </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>-log⁡</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:sSubPr><m:ctrlPr><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr></m:ctrlPr></m:sSubPr><m:e><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>p</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>θ</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Cambria Math" w:eastAsia="Cambria Math" w:hAnsi="Cambria Math" w:cs="Cambria Math"/></w:rPr><m:t>(x)</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> of the training data. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="03EBE013" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRPr="00414334" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/><w:rPr><w:b/><w:bCs/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">At operation {{fig}}25, the system updates parameters of the model based on the comparison. For example, parameters of a U-Net may be updated using gradient descent. Time-dependent parameters of the Gaussian transitions can also be learned.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

paragraphs: <w:p w14:paraId="0AFFFE5D" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">FIG. {{FIG:16}} shows an example of a computing device {{fig}}00 according to aspects of the present disclosure. The example shown includes computing device {{fig}}00, processor(s) {{fig}}05, memory subsystem {{fig}}10, communication interface {{fig}}15, I/O interface {{fig}}20, user interface component(s), and channel {{fig}}30. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">In some embodiments, computing device {{fig}}00 is an example of, or includes aspects of, a media processing apparatus as described in FIGs. {{FIG:1}} and {{FIG:2}}. In some embodiments, computing device {{fig}}00 includes one or more processors {{fig}}05 are configured to execute instructions stored in memory subsystem {{fig}}10 to // CLAIM 1 FEATURES //.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="0DAB07CC" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">According to some aspects, computing device {{fig}}00 includes one or more processors {{fig}}05. In some cases, a processor is an intelligent hardware device, (e.g., a general-purpose processing component, a digital signal processor (DSP), a central processing unit (CPU), a graphics processing unit (GPU), a microcontroller, an application specific integrated circuit (ASIC), a field programmable gate array (FPGA), a programmable logic device, a discrete gate or transistor logic component, a discrete hardware component, or a combination thereof. In some cases, a processor is configured to operate a memory array using a memory controller. In other cases, a memory controller is integrated into a processor. In some cases, a processor is configured to execute computer-readable instructions stored in a memory to perform various functions. In some embodiments, a processor includes special purpose components for modem processing, baseband processing, digital signal processing, or transmission processing. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="7556D228" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">According to some aspects, memory subsystem {{fig}}10 includes one or more memory devices. Examples of a memory device include random access memory (RAM), read-only memory (ROM), or a hard disk. Examples of memory devices include solid state memory and a hard disk drive. In some examples, memory is used to store computer-readable, computer-executable software including instructions that, when executed, cause a processor to perform various functions described herein. The memory may store model parameters in the form of tensors which, when combined with mathematical operations such as matrix multiplications, implement machine learning models specially configured to perform specific tasks. These </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidRPr="007D2403"><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>parameters may correspond to the models described with reference to FIG. {{FIG:2}}. In some cases, the memory contains, among other things, a basic input/output system (BIOS) which controls basic hardware or software operation such as the interaction with peripheral components or devices. In some cases, a memory controller operates memory cells. For example, the memory controller can include a row decoder, column decoder, or both. In some cases, memory cells within a memory store information in the form of a logical state</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="1EC93973" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">According to some aspects, communication interface {{fig}}15 operates at a boundary between communicating entities (such as computing device {{fig}}00, one or more user devices, a cloud, and one or more databases) and channel {{fig}}30 and can record and process communications. In some cases, communication interface {{fig}}15 is provided to enable a processing system coupled to a transceiver (e.g., a transmitter and/or a receiver). In some examples, the transceiver is configured to transmit (or send) and receive signals for a communications device via an antenna.</w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="28ADC06E" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Numbering"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">According to some aspects, I/O interface {{fig}}20 is controlled by an I/O controller to manage input and output signals for computing device {{fig}}00. In some cases, I/O interface {{fig}}20 manages peripherals not integrated into computing device {{fig}}00. In some cases, I/O interface {{fig}}20 represents a physical connection or port to an external peripheral. In some cases, the I/O controller uses an operating system such as iOS®, ANDROID®, MS-DOS®, MS-WINDOWS®, OS/2®, UNIX®, LINUX®, or other known operating system. In some cases, the I/O controller represents or interacts with a modem, a keyboard, a mouse, a touchscreen, or a similar device. In some cases, the I/O controller is implemented as a component of a processor. In some cases, a user interacts with a device via I/O interface {{fig}}20 or via hardware components controlled by the I/O controller. </w:t></w:r></w:p>

<w:p w14:paraId="2CBBF2A9" w14:textId="77777777" w:rsidR="00555F37" w:rsidRDefault="00555F37" w:rsidP="00555F37"><w:pPr><w:numPr><w:ilvl w:val="0"/><w:numId w:val="1"/></w:numPr><w:tabs><w:tab w:val="left" w:pos="1080"/></w:tabs><w:spacing w:before="160" w:line="480" w:lineRule="auto"/><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:lastRenderedPageBreak/><w:t>According to some aspects, user interface component(s) {{fig}}25 enable a user to interact with computing device {{fig}}00. In some cases, user interface component(s) {{fig}}25 include an audio device, such as an external speaker system, an external display device such as a display screen, an input device (e.g., a remote control device interfaced with a user interface directly or through the I/O controller), or a combination thereof. In some cases, user interface component(s) {{fig}}25 include a GUI.</w:t></w:r></w:p>
